lessons.title: Deglobalization or Slowbalisation? What the Trade Data Actually Shows

children.text: Every earnings call now carries some version of the same sentence: "we are diversifying our supply chain away from single-country concentration." Every finance ministry speech carries some version of "de-risking, not decoupling." The language of the last two lessons, reshoring, friendshoring, fragmentation, has become so common in market commentary that it is worth stopping and asking a plain question before going further: has world trade actually shrunk? A macro investor who answers that question wrong will misprice an entire portfolio of assumptions. The honest answer, once you look at the actual data instead of the headlines, is more precise and more useful than either "globalization is over" or "nothing has changed."

body.text: World trade has not shrunk. It has been rerouted, and it has become more expensive to conduct across certain borders. That distinction, rerouting versus shrinking, is the single most important thing the data shows, and it is what separates slowbalisation from a genuine reversal of globalization.

children.text: What the Aggregate Data Shows: A Plateau, Not a Collapse

World trade in goods and services, measured as a share of global GDP, peaked around 61% in 2008. If deglobalization in the literal sense, trade actively reversing, were happening, this ratio should be falling steadily. It is not. It dipped sharply during the 2020 COVID shock, then rebounded to levels close to the 2008 peak by 2022, helped in part by a spike in commodity prices that inflated the value of trade in energy and food.

body.title: World Trade (Goods and Services) as a Share of GDP, 2008-2023

children.text: Read that chart carefully. A line bouncing in a band roughly between 52% and 63% over fifteen years is not a system unwinding. It is a system that stopped climbing after decades of near-uninterrupted growth, exactly what "slowbalisation" describes, and exactly what you would expect if the four shocks from the previous lesson had raised the cost and risk of trade without destroying the underlying economic logic for it.

body.text: Do not mistake a flat aggregate ratio for "nothing has changed." The composition underneath that flat line is shifting hard, and that shift is exactly what shows up next in this lesson, and in every chapter that follows.

children.text: Where the Real Change Is: Rerouting, Not Reduction

The clearest evidence sits in bilateral trade data, specifically who the United States buys from. China's share of total US goods imports fell from roughly 21.6% in 2017 to roughly 13.9% in 2023, its lowest level since 2004. If this were a story of America simply importing less, the story would end there. It does not.

markDefs.definition: A country that gains a growing share of a large importer's trade partly by absorbing manufacturing and assembly shifted away from a country facing tariffs or restrictions, often while itself importing more intermediate inputs from that same restricted country.

children.text: Total US goods imports did not fall anywhere near as much as China's share did. The demand did not disappear, it moved to Mexico and Vietnam in particular, which economists increasingly describe as

. And that is where the data gets more interesting: Vietnam and Mexico have both simultaneously increased their own imports of components and intermediate goods from China over the same period. A meaningful share of what looks like "decoupling from China" in US import statistics is, underneath, Chinese-made inputs being assembled one or two borders away before reaching an American port. This is trade diversion and supply chain lengthening, not trade disappearing.

body.title: Measure the reroute
body.prompt: China's share of US goods imports fell from approximately 21.6% in 2017 to approximately 13.9% in 2023. What is that decline in percentage points?
body.explanation: 21.6 minus 13.9 is approximately 7.7 percentage points. That is a large shift in a major bilateral trading relationship, but it needs to be read alongside Mexico's and Vietnam's rising shares, not in isolation, before concluding that trade itself has contracted.

children.text: FDI Data Tells an Even Sharper Story

If trade flows show rerouting, investment flows show something closer to genuine bifurcation. IMF research following the 2022 Russia-Ukraine shock found that greenfield foreign direct investment between countries on opposite sides of major geopolitical divides has grown more slowly than FDI between countries on the same side, a pattern that barely existed before 2018. Capital, unlike a container of goods, commits for a decade or more. Investors deciding where to build a new factory are pricing geopolitical alignment into that decision in a way importers deciding where to buy a shipment this quarter are not, which is exactly why FDI data moves first and trade data catches up later.

body.title: The Headline Claim vs What the Data Shows

columns.label: "Deglobalization" headline claim
points: Global trade is shrinking as a share of the economy
Companies are simply importing less from abroad
The world is retreating into self-sufficiency

columns.label: What the underlying data shows
points: Trade/GDP is flat near multi-decade highs, not falling
Import demand is being rerouted through connector countries, not eliminated
Supply chains are lengthening and adding intermediate steps, not shortening
FDI is bifurcating along geopolitical lines faster than trade itself

children.text: Why This Distinction Matters for How You Invest

If you believed the literal "deglobalization" story, you would position for a shrinking global trade pie and underweight anything tied to cross-border commerce. The data says something more specific and more tradeable: the pie is roughly the same size, but the routes through it have changed, and companies positioned as new connector points capture growth that companies clinging to the old routes lose. On NSE and BSE, this shows up directly in how you screen for opportunity. A company whose export revenue mix has shifted toward the US and EU as China's own export share to those markets has fallen is benefiting from exactly the reroute this lesson describes, a pattern worth checking directly in company filings or a tool like screener.in when you build a watchlist for the sector work later in this course.

body.title: Rerouting or reduction?
body.question: Vietnam's imports of components from China have risen at the same time as Vietnam's exports to the US have risen. What does this combination most strongly suggest?
options: Vietnam has replaced China as a manufacturing power independent of China
Vietnam is acting as a connector, assembling Chinese-made inputs before shipping to the US
The US and China have fully decoupled from each other
body.explanation: Rising Chinese input imports into Vietnam alongside rising Vietnamese exports to the US is the textbook signature of a connector country: goods and components are taking a longer route to the same end market, rather than that trade disappearing or China's manufacturing base being genuinely displaced.

cards.definition: The post-2008 pattern of world trade/GDP plateauing near record highs rather than continuing to climb or collapsing outright.

A country, such as Vietnam or Mexico, that gains import share from a restricted trading partner while itself importing more inputs from that same partner, effectively rerouting trade rather than replacing it.
The shift of trade flows from one supplying country to another because of tariffs, sanctions or sourcing decisions, without a proportional change in total global demand.
The pattern, documented by IMF research since 2022, of foreign direct investment growing faster between geopolitically aligned countries than between countries on opposite sides of major divides.

points: World trade as a share of global GDP is flat near multi-decade highs, not falling, which rules out a literal reading of "deglobalization."
China's share of US goods imports fell from roughly 21.6% in 2017 to roughly 13.9% in 2023, but Mexico and Vietnam absorbed most of that share, rather than US total imports shrinking.
Vietnam and Mexico have simultaneously increased their own imports of Chinese components, evidence that much of the shift is rerouting and supply chain lengthening, not a clean break from China.

Foreign direct investment is bifurcating along geopolitical lines faster than trade flows are, since capital commits for years and prices in alignment risk earlier than a single quarter's import order does.
The accurate term for what the data shows is slowbalisation and fragmentation, a rerouting and rising cost of trade, not deglobalization in the literal sense of trade shrinking.
For investors, this distinction is directly tradeable: identify which companies and countries are becoming new connector points, since that is where the growth in the rerouted trade is landing.

Trade and FDI figures are presented as commonly cited approximations for teaching purposes and should be verified against primary sources such as US Census Bureau trade data, the World Bank and IMF research before use in professional analysis.
